label: NanoSwitch
description: NanoSwitch (N-SW) - 4x 1G RJ45: one 24V passive PoE-in socket that powers the unit, three 24V passive PoE passthrough sockets (24 W per port, 30 W total across the three).

poe.note: 30 W is the vendor's total, not a per-port figure: techspecs 'Total passive PoE Max. Wattaget' = '24V, 2-pair, 1A for 3 ports (30W)' beside 'Passive PoE Max. Wattage per port' = '24V, 2-pair, 1A per port (24W)'. Three sockets at 24 W each reach 72 W, so the aggregate is what has to bind here; the 24 W per-port ceiling alone would let two full loads through.

notes: Vendor figures from Ubiquiti's tech-spec page for this SKU (`https://techspecs.ui.com/uisp/wired/n-sw`, HTTP 200, 575,565 B, server-rendered `<td class="key">` table, crawler user-agent, read 2026-11-21): `Networking interface = (4) GbE RJ45 ports [(1) PoE-in, (3) PoE passthrough]`, `Power method = Passive 24V, 2-pair PoE-in`, `Supported voltage range = 21.6-30V`, `Power consumption = Typical: 1.5W / Max.: 30W`, `Power supply = POE-24-30W-G PoE adapter (Not included)`, `Passive PoE Max. Wattage per port = 24V, 2-pair, 1A per port (24W)`, `Total passive PoE Max. Wattaget = 24V, 2-pair, 1A for 3 ports (30W)`. The row had shipped the four sockets as three bare `poeOut: true` plus one with no power field at all: the bare direction bit is what `Device.poeDraw()` (engine/device.js) adds as **1 W** and what `pseDraw()` (engine/validation.js) sums, so all three passthrough sockets fully loaded made `poeDraw()` answer 3 W, and with no `poe.budgetW` the faceplate said the budget was not modelled at all. Each passthrough socket now declares the vendor's 24 W per-port ceiling and `poe.budgetW` is the vendor's 30 W aggregate; three 24 W loads (72 W) are now refused with E_POE_BUDGET instead of accepted at 3 W. The sockets are 24 V **passive**, so `poeOutClass` is `passive`, not `PoE`/802.3af as it read before: the vendor prints `Power method: Passive 24V` and offers no negotiation, so a standard 802.3af/at PD will not come up on them. The PD socket is `eth3` and carries `poeIn: 1.5`, the vendor's typical consumption; that is the whole of what the engine can bill, because a passthrough switch forwards its downstream load rather than drawing it, and `poeIn` is a static per-port figure. The vendor prints no port numbers (only `(1) PoE-in, (3) PoE passthrough`), so this pass fixed the count, the wattages and the class without renumbering the panel: the three sockets that already carried `poeOut` stay the PSE sockets and the fourth becomes the input.
